subject: Interpreting fator correlations in exploratory factor analysis

messages.author: 1ff81ef1259d6923
messages.subject: Interpreting fator correlations in exploratory factor analysis
parts:
Hi Phil and everyone in the group,

I have been looking for postings about this question in the group and I couldn't find any. 

I am doing an exploratory factor analysis just like the example in your article "mirt: A Multidimensional Item Response Theory Package for the R Environment". 

R> summary(mod2, rotate = "oblimin", suppress = 0.25)
Rotation: oblimin
Rotated factor loadings:
F_1 F_2 h2
Item.1 NA -0.711 0.493
Item.2 0.545 NA 0.305
Item.3 0.759 NA 0.572
Item.4 NA -0.292 0.180
Item.5 NA -0.307 0.173
Factor correlations:
F_1 F_2
F_1 1.000 -0.591
F_2 -0.591 1.000

I am wondering how to interpret the correlations here between F_1, F_2 (-0.591). What method was used to generate this correlations, how to interpret (-0.591 demonstrates negative, moderate corerlations?), and if we could identified the significance p-value for this correlations. 

Thank you very much! 

Best,
Yuanjin

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Interpreting fator correlations in exploratory factor analysis
parts:
Hi Yuanjin,

For exploratory models mirt is generally less concerned with providing p-values for standardized coefficients, largely because of the rotational indeterminacy in the such models. If necessary, you could try to repeat the analysis using bootstrapping to obtain an empirical estimate of the variability of these correlations and go from there, but for exploratory models this is likely less interesting and useful. As an aside, I would generally call a correlation of .59 moderate, just like any other correlation estimate, though that's a little devoid of meaning without additional context (this might be extremely small if, for example, the test was supposed to have high correlations between factors, like general and specific math). HTH.

Phil
